title: argus chain card
description: One chain that worked, derived from a confirmed finding and the probes that reached it. A card exists to make the second run against a stack cheaper than the first: it says what the stack looked like, where the input was, which ladder steps fired, which probe first discriminated, and what shape of proof settled it. It is deliberately useless as a shortcut past proof — it carries no target, no credential, no extracted row and no proof output, so reusing it can only produce a hypothesis, never a finding. `argus/knowledge/chains.py` reads this file: the property list here is the allowed-key list the validator enforces, so a field added to a card without being added here is refused rather than silently stored.

schema.description: card schema version; 1 is the only one that exists.

slug.description: the card's filename stem, and its identity in the corpus: class, entry-point shape, leading stack product, and eight characters of source_digest. It names a shape, never a target.

title.description: one line a model reads first: the class, the entry-point shape and the product it was found on.

vuln_class.description: a class in the proof matrix. A card for a class the matrix does not know is refused, because there would be no requirement to reuse it under.

severity.description: the severity the finding carried. A default from the matrix, not a measurement of this target's exposure.

stack.description: what the service was observed to be running. Server banner, declared framework markers, version strings, and the normalised markers `match` compares against a new target. A page title and a content type are deliberately absent: both change with the deployment, so matching on them ranks the wrong cards first.

framework.description: framework markers the fingerprint named, e.g. django, laravel, tomcat.

versions.description: product/version pairs observed in the banners, e.g. werkzeug/2.0.1.

markers.description: normalised `product:`, `version:` and `major:` markers. These are what scoring compares, and a card with none of them is unmatchable and refused.

entry_point.description: where the input was, never what was put in it. The parameter name and its location are the shape worth reusing; the payload that worked is not, because a payload reused without re-proving is exactly the shortcut this card must not offer.

location.description: query, body, header, cookie, path, or unknown.

param.description: the parameter or field name, as observed.

method.description: the HTTP method, when the finding recorded one.

path_shape.description: the request path with numeric and identifier-shaped segments replaced by :id.

note.description: one line on how the value reached the sink, in the words of the hypothesis that was confirmed.

steps.description: the probes that actually fired against this hypothesis, in the order the ledger recorded them, with the ladder step each one was. This is the cheap half of the card: it shows which steps were needed and which were skipped on a stack of this shape. It is required and may be empty: a finding proven through ledger.add_evidence alone — a proxy request, a browser session, a source read — has no broker probes, and an empty list says that honestly where an absent key would read as a forgotten field.

step.description: the ladder step name, or empty when the probe named none.

tier.description: the risk tier the ladder gives this step.

result.description: signal, no-signal, error or refused, as recorded.

first_discriminating_probe.description: the first probe that came back `signal`. It is the one to run first on a new target of this shape, because it is the one that was observed to separate this stack from a stack where the class is absent.

why.description: the ladder's reason for the step, or a statement that no probe on this hypothesis returned a signal.

proof.description: the shape of proof that settled it, and the requirement it had to meet. The check names are carried; the check details are not, because those hold the nonce, the identity line and the table that were the proof.

kind.description: the proof matrix verifier shape, e.g. command_output, data_extraction, file_read.

requirement.description: the class requirement, copied from the matrix so the card cannot be read as having met it.

checks_passed.description: the names of the checks that passed on the original finding. Names only.

preconditions.description: plain language, one line each: what has to be true of a new target before this chain is worth a probe. Nothing checks them for you, which is why `match` also reports the markers the card needs and the target has not been seen to have.

blast_radius.description: what reusing this chain can damage on a shared instance. Derived from the proof shape, not measured on the original target: it states what the class puts in reach, so that the decision to go past the benign proof is made by a human who read it.

reuse.description: the standing caveat: a match is a candidate, and the class's proof requirement is unchanged by the card existing.

source_digest.description: sha256 of engagement name and finding id, truncated. It makes a card traceable by whoever still has the engagement, and carries neither the engagement's name nor the client's. `harvest` uses it to tell an already-written card from a new one.

recorded.description: when the card was written, ISO-8601 UTC.

x-must-not-carry: the target's hostname or address — a card is about a shape, and a shape that names a host invites the next agent to probe that host
any credential, in any field — the ledger stores a secret's kind and position, and a card does not even store that
any extracted row — five rows is a proof for the engagement that took them, and a corpus of other people's rows is a breach with a schema
any flag-shaped string — it is the answer to someone's exercise, not knowledge about a stack
the proof output itself — a nonce, a uid= line or a dumped table in a card is a claim that the card has proven something, which it has not
a payload that worked — the entry-point shape is reusable, the literal value is a shortcut past the class's proof

x-refusals.unknown-field: a key the schema does not declare, at any depth. A card is read by agents that trust it; an undeclared field is unreviewed content in a trusted file, and the obvious place to park the payload that worked is a key inside a step.
x-refusals.missing-field: a required key absent, or empty. An empty field reads as 'there was nothing here' rather than 'this was not written'. `steps` is the exception: a finding proven through ledger.add_evidence alone has no broker probes, and refusing it would make the corpus a record of what the broker ran rather than of what was proven.
x-refusals.type: a value whose type the schema does not declare, including an item of the wrong type inside a declared array. A marker that is not a string is the shape that makes ranking raise rather than refuse.
x-refusals.schema-version: a card version this reader does not know.
x-refusals.bad-slug: a slug that is not 1-100 characters of a-z 0-9 . _ - starting alphanumeric. The slug becomes a filename, so it is checked rather than trusted.
x-refusals.refused-class: the class is one the proof matrix refuses to prove at all, the way `dos` is. The corpus is checked in and outlives the engagement, so it is the one route by which a refused class could return as a ranked suggestion with steps under it.
x-refusals.forbidden-field: a key from x-forbidden-field-names. These are the field names the evidence records use for the things a card must not carry, so the name alone is enough to refuse.
x-refusals.secret-shape: text that argus.util.redact rewrites, an Authorization-shaped assignment, or a private key header.
x-refusals.address-literal: an IPv4 or IPv6 literal, or an absolute URL. A card needs neither, and both name a target.
x-refusals.proof-output: a uid=/whoami line, an /etc/passwd row, or a probe nonce.
x-refusals.engagement-hostname: a host named by the engagement's targets or scope, or the engagement's own name.
x-refusals.unmatchable: no stack marker, so the card can never be ranked against a target and would only ever be read by accident.
x-refusals.not-confirmed: the finding is a candidate. A card records what settled; a candidate's chain is the part that did not.
x-refusals.class-not-in-matrix: the class has no proof requirement here, so there is nothing to reuse the card under.
x-refusals.over-long: a field or a card past its bound. Bounded collection applies to what is written down as well as to what is read.
x-refusals.could-not-write: not a judgement about the card: the finding could not be read, or the corpus file could not be written. Reported per finding so that a harvest reports the cards it did write.
